items.title: 71542_Bill Coleman autobiographical manuscript
items.q: Later I got to know the other musicians who were Edgar Sampson, alto sax... I had never seen or heard about these musicians but when they started their first number, I knew that it was an orchestra that had something to say... this orchestra was under the leadership of Arthur Gibbs.

ctx.x: There were always some kind of musicians playing those shows and a couple of comedians. Some of the jokes were: How do you feel, Mr. Bones? and Mr. Bones would answer: Just like a stove! The other one would ask: How's that? and Mr. Bones would answer: Red hot and still a heating.

Another one was: How do you feel to-night, Mr. Sampson? Mr. Sampson would say: Just like that woman's mouth, and point to some woman in the crowd. The other one who was usually known as the straight man would ask: How's that? and Sampson would say: wide open.

A group of these medicine shows would travel from city to city and play in different parts of the town and I heard about one that was playing in a district which was quite some distance from where we lived and that had a family of musicians working with them. The trumpet player was called Gabriel and I was told that he was very good. We had moved again and were now living on lower Carlisle Avenue, two blocks from where the red light district was.
